headline: The Siding Installation Supervisor Foundation
threshold: By Lesson 10, you can greet your siding crew, give numbers, times and measurements in feet and inches, describe walls and tools, ask simple questions, make polite requests and get help, and start Siding Installation Supervisor Lesson 1.

lessons.title: Sounds and Greetings
lessons.objective: Pronounce Spanish vowels and key sounds and greet your siding crew at the start of the day.
lessons.focus: The five vowels, ch, j, ll, rr and the written accent; greetings and introductions

words.note: ll sounds like the y in yes: mar-TEE-yo.
Every vowel is short and clear: es-ca-LE-ra.
ch sounds like the ch in church.
j sounds like a strong English h: CA-ha.
j is a strong h: HE-fe. A woman boss is la jefa.
rr is a rolled, trilled r.
Stress falls on the last syllable: pa-RED.
The written accent marks the stressed syllable: LA-piz.

words.en: My name is Carlos and I'm the supervisor.
words.es: Me llamo Carlos y soy el supervisor.
words.note: A woman says soy la supervisora.

words.en: Nice to meet you, what's your name?
words.note: Usted is formal; use it with someone new.

words.en: How do you say this in Spanish?

lessons.speaking: Greet a crew member at the truck, say your name and role, and ask how to say hammer, ladder and level in Spanish.

lessons.title: Numbers, Time and Measurements
lessons.objective: Say numbers, times and simple siding measurements in feet and inches to your crew.
lessons.focus: Numbers 0 to 1,000, clock time with a las, and feet, inches, pieces and packages

words.note: The unit of length; plural los pies.
Many crews just say la cinta.

words.en: We start at 7 in the morning.
words.es: Empezamos a las 7 de la mañana.
La pared mide 24 pies de largo.

words.note: Use son las for times from 2 on; es la una for 1.

lessons.speaking: Tell a crew member the start time, the break time, and the length of one wall in feet and inches.

lessons.title: Ser and Estar
lessons.objective: Say who people are and describe the condition of walls, scaffolds and panels on the job.
lessons.focus: ser for what something or someone is, estar for its condition or location

words.note: Estar listo means ready; listos for a group.
A woman helper is la ayudante.
estar: a condition that can change.
The adjective agrees: pared is feminine, so mojada.

words.en: This is Juan, the new helper.
words.es: Él es Juan, el ayudante nuevo.
words.note: ser: who someone is.

words.en: I'm the supervisor on this job.
words.es: Soy el supervisor de esta obra.

lessons.speaking: Introduce a new helper to a crew member, then say whether the scaffold is safe and the wall is wet or clean.

lessons.title: Have, There Is, Need and Want
lessons.objective: Say what the crew has, what there is on site, and what you need or want for the job.
lessons.focus: tener, hay, necesitar, querer and hay que + infinitive

words.note: Feminine word with el before it: el agua fría.
Tú is informal, between coworkers.
Hay means there is or there are.

words.en: I need the extension cord, please.
I want to see the wall first.
You have to wear safety glasses.
words.es: Hay que usar lentes de seguridad.
words.note: Hay que + infinitive: a general rule for everyone.

words.en: You have to check the ladder before going up.
words.es: Hay que revisar la escalera antes de subir.

lessons.speaking: Ask a coworker if they have gloves and a hard hat, say what you need from the truck, and state one safety rule with hay que.

lessons.title: Go, Do and Can
lessons.objective: Tell the crew where you are going, what you will do today, and what you can or can't do.
lessons.focus: ir, ir a + infinitive for plans, hacer, and poder

words.en: I'm going to the store for more nails.
words.es: Voy a la tienda por más clavos.

words.en: We're going to start on the front.
words.es: Vamos a empezar por el frente.
words.note: ir a + infinitive talks about a plan.

words.en: Today we're going to do the back.
words.es: Hoy vamos a hacer la parte de atrás.

words.en: I can finish this side today.
I can't go up without a hard hat.
What are you going to do tomorrow?

lessons.speaking: Tell a crew lead which side of the house you will do today, where you are going now, and what you can finish later.

lessons.title: Present Tense
lessons.objective: Say what you, your coworkers and the crew do every day on a siding job.
lessons.focus: Present tense of regular -ar, -er and -ir verbs for yo, tú, usted, nosotros and ellos

words.en: I measure and you mark the line.
words.es: Yo mido y tú marcas la línea.
words.note: Medir changes e to i: mido, mides, but medimos.

words.en: You work with Luis at the window.
words.es: Usted trabaja con Luis en la ventana.

words.en: We clean up the trash at 4.
words.es: Nosotros limpiamos la basura a las 4.

words.en: They cut the panels on the table.
words.es: Ellos cortan los paneles en la mesa.

words.en: Do you write down the measurements?
words.note: -ir verbs: escribo, escribes, escribe, escribimos, escriben.

lessons.speaking: Tell a coworker who measures, who marks the line and who cuts, and say what time the crew cleans up the trash.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.objective: Ask simple questions about people, places, times and amounts on the job site.
lessons.focus: Question words: qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cuánto, cómo, por qué, cuál

words.note: For more than one person: ¿quiénes?
It agrees: cuántos paneles, cuánta agua.
The answer uses porque, one word: because.

words.es: ¿Quién tiene la llave de la casa?

words.en: How many panels are left to do?
words.note: Faltar means still needed or missing.

lessons.speaking: Ask a crew member where the restroom is, who has the house key, and when the material arrives.

lessons.title: No, Never and How Much
lessons.objective: Say no, never, nobody, nothing and not yet, and ask for more, less or another piece.
lessons.focus: no, nunca, nadie, nada, todavía no, más, menos and otro

words.note: Spanish uses a double negative: no hay nada.
Never say un otro: otro clavo, otra pieza.
Masculine even though it ends in -a.

words.es: No hay nadie en el andamio.

words.en: Never cut without a dust mask.
words.note: Corten is the ustedes command, for the whole crew.

words.en: We haven't finished this wall yet.
I need another piece, this one is damaged.
words.es: Necesito otra pieza, esta está dañada.

words.en: Leave more of a gap, according to the manufacturer.
words.es: Dejen más espacio, según el fabricante.

lessons.speaking: Tell a crew member the wall isn't finished yet, ask for another piece because one is damaged, and say nobody cuts without a mask.

lessons.title: Polite Requests and Commands
lessons.objective: Make polite requests to a homeowner and give simple usted commands to one worker.
lessons.focus: ¿Puede…? requests and usted commands for everyday verbs

words.note: For a woman; a man is el cliente.

words.en: Can you move your car out of the driveway, please?
words.es: ¿Puede mover su carro de la entrada, por favor?
words.note: ¿Puede…? with usted is polite with a homeowner.

words.en: Can you bring your dog into the house?
words.es: ¿Puede meter a su perro a la casa?

words.en: Put the tarp over the plants.
words.es: Ponga la lona sobre las plantas.
words.note: Usted command to one worker: ponga, from poner.

words.en: Call me if you have a question.

lessons.speaking: Ask a homeowner politely to move the car and bring the dog inside, then tell one worker to put the tarp over the plants.

lessons.title: Words You Already Know and Getting Help
lessons.objective: Recognize Spanish words you already know and ask for help or repetition on the job.
lessons.focus: Cognates ending in -ción, -dad and -ente, plus survival phrases for getting help

words.note: -ción words are feminine and match English -tion.
-dad words are feminine and often match English -ty.

words.en: I don't understand, can you repeat, please?

words.note: Llamen is the ustedes command, for everyone nearby.

lessons.speaking: Tell a crew member you speak a little Spanish, ask them to repeat slowly, and ask what one safety word means.
